title: “VENGEANCE IS MINE”: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT GOD IS ASKING YOU TO SURRENDER WHEN SOMEONE HAS DESTROYED YOUR PEACE
paragraphs: “VENGEANCE IS MINE”: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT GOD IS ASKING YOU TO SURRENDER WHEN SOMEONE HAS DESTROYED YOUR PEACE

You prayed for justice. You waited for an apology. You watched the person who wounded you continue living as though nothing happened. But what if the most dangerous thing they left behind wasn't the pain they caused you—but the revenge slowly taking possession of your heart?
There is a kind of pain that doesn't leave bruises on your skin.
It leaves questions in your prayers.

It makes you stare at the ceiling at two in the morning, replaying conversations that ended months ago. It makes your stomach tighten when you hear a certain name. It turns familiar places into reminders of something you desperately wish had never happened.
And sometimes, the most unbearable part isn't what someone did to you.
It's watching them walk away.
No confession.
No apology.
No visible consequences.
They still laugh. They still post pictures. They still receive congratulations. Sometimes they even speak about God as though they never shattered someone else's world.
Meanwhile, you're trying to remember what it feels like to sleep without carrying a courtroom inside your chest.
And somewhere in the silence, a question rises that you're almost afraid to say aloud.
"Lord, did You see what they did to me?"
You know what Scripture says about forgiveness. You've heard sermons about loving your enemies. You've probably told other people to trust God's timing.
But knowing the right Bible verse and surviving the wrong someone committed against you are two very different experiences.
Because when the wound is yours, justice stops being a theological subject.
It becomes personal.
You want the truth exposed.
You want them to understand what they did.
You want someone, somewhere, to acknowledge that what happened was wrong.
And perhaps, if you're being painfully honest, there are moments when you want them to hurt the way you hurt.
Then you encounter four words that seem to stand between your suffering and your desire for justice.
"Vengeance is mine."
Romans 12:19.
But what does God actually mean?
Is He telling you to forget what happened? To remain silent? To allow evil to continue? To pretend the person who betrayed you deserves no consequences?
Or is there something far deeper happening in this command—something that could save your soul from becoming a prisoner of the very injustice you survived?
Because here's the part we often miss.
When God tells you to surrender vengeance, He is not asking you to surrender the truth. He is asking you to surrender the throne.
And understanding that difference may change the way you carry your pain for the rest of your life.
The apostle Paul writes:
—Romans 12:19, KJV
The Greek text contains these words:
ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω
Emoi ekdikēsis, egō antapodōsō.
A faithful rendering is:
"Vengeance belongs to Me; I will repay."
The word ekdikēsis refers to vengeance or the administration of justice against wrongdoing. It is not merely an emotional outburst. In this context, it concerns the rightful response to evil.
And antapodōsō, from the verb antapodidōmi, means "I will repay" or "I will give back in return."
Notice what God does not say.
He does not say evil is imaginary.
He does not say betrayal is insignificant.
He does not say the guilty are automatically innocent because you have chosen to forgive them.
He says repayment belongs to Him.
Paul is drawing from Deuteronomy 32:35, where the Hebrew declares:
לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם
Li naqam veshillem.
"Vengeance is Mine, and recompense."
The Hebrew naqam concerns vengeance or retribution, while shillem concerns repayment or recompense. The wording emphasizes that the right to administer ultimate retribution belongs to God.
This is not a promise that God will punish your offender in the particular way you imagine, on the schedule you demand, or within your lifetime.
It is a declaration that justice has an Owner.
And that Owner is not you.
There is something deeply humbling about that truth.
Because revenge often begins with a legitimate wound.
Someone really did lie.
Someone really did abandon you.
Someone really did manipulate, exploit, humiliate, betray, or abuse your trust.
Your grief may be entirely justified.
But somewhere along the way, a desire for justice can become a hunger for control.
You begin imagining what they deserve.
You rehearse what you would say if you had the opportunity.
You hope someone will expose them.
You check whether their life is falling apart.
You quietly measure God's faithfulness by whether their suffering has finally begun.
And without realizing it, the person who wounded you has become the center of your emotional universe.
They are no longer physically present, but they still influence your mood.
They no longer speak to you, but you still argue with them in your mind.
They may have moved on, but a part of your life remains suspended at the moment they betrayed you.
That is one of the hidden tragedies of revenge.
The person who hurt you once can continue occupying your heart long after the original injury.
And Jesus loves you too much to leave you there.
But before we go further, something needs to be said clearly.
Forgiveness is not permission for someone to continue hurting you.
Surrendering vengeance does not mean refusing to report abuse, declining lawful protection, ignoring criminal wrongdoing, or returning to an unsafe relationship.
Romans 12:19 forbids personal retaliation. It does not abolish accountability.
In fact, only a few verses later, Romans 13:1–4 describes governing authorities as having a responsibility to restrain and punish wrongdoing.
The same apostle who tells believers not to avenge themselves recognizes a legitimate public role for justice.
That matters.
Especially for the person who has been told to remain silent in the name of Christianity.
Especially for the woman pressured to return to danger because someone quoted a verse about forgiveness.
Especially for the child, the vulnerable person, or the betrayed believer who has been made to feel that speaking the truth is somehow dishonoring God.
No.
Biblical forgiveness does not require protecting an offender from rightful consequences.
You can forgive and establish boundaries.
You can forgive and seek legal protection.
You can forgive and refuse reconciliation where repentance, safety, and trust are absent.
You can forgive and still tell the truth.
Jesus never commanded His followers to rename evil as good.
He calls us to overcome evil with good.
And that is a very different thing.
Perhaps you remember Joseph.
The young man whose own brothers hated him so intensely that they sold him into slavery.
Imagine that betrayal.
Not strangers.
Not enemies from another nation.
His own brothers.
The people who knew his childhood. The people who shared his father's home. The people who should have protected him.
They stripped him of his freedom and sold him into an uncertain future.
Joseph was taken into Egypt, falsely accused, and imprisoned.
Years passed.
The Bible doesn't tell us every thought that crossed his mind during those lonely nights.
But it tells us enough to know that his suffering was real.
And then, through God's providence, Joseph rose to a position of extraordinary authority.
Eventually, the very brothers who betrayed him stood before him, needing the food he had power to provide.
Think about that moment.
Joseph had something most wounded people never receive.
The opportunity to make his offenders feel powerless.
He could have humiliated them.
He could have made them beg.
He could have used his authority to settle the score.
And who would have been surprised?
But when his brothers feared retaliation after their father's death, Joseph said something astonishing.
"Fear not: for am I in the place of God?"
—Genesis 50:19, KJV
There it is again.
The throne.
The place of God.
Joseph did not pretend the betrayal had been harmless. In the very next verse, he acknowledged their intention:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good..."
—Genesis 50:20, KJV
Read that carefully.
Their intention was evil. God's providence was good.
The good God brought from Joseph's suffering did not make his brothers' evil righteous.
God's sovereignty did not excuse their betrayal.
And Joseph's mercy did not require rewriting history.
He named the wrong.
Then he refused to appoint himself as the ultimate judge.
What extraordinary freedom.
Not freedom because the past never happened.
Freedom because the past no longer had authority to determine the kind of man he would become.
Somebody reading this needs to hear that.
You do not have to become cruel to prove that what happened to you was cruel.
You do not have to become dishonest because someone lied about you.
You do not have to become heartless because someone treated your heart carelessly.
You do not have to become the thing that wounded you.
And you do not need to call revenge "justice" simply because your pain is real.
God sees the difference.
But perhaps your heart is resisting right now.
Because Joseph's story is beautiful when you're reading it from the safety of your living room.
It feels different when you're the one still living with the consequences of someone else's sin.
What about the person who never apologizes?
What about the spouse who betrayed the marriage and then blamed you?
What about the friend who exposed your secrets?
What about the church leader who used spiritual language to manipulate you?
What about the family member who wounded you and now expects you to behave as though nothing happened?
What about the person whose choices cost you years you can never recover?
What about the injustice that changed your entire life?
Does God expect you to smile through all of it?
No.
Look at the Psalms.
David cried out to God about betrayal, persecution, fear, and injustice.
In Psalm 55, he describes the anguish of being betrayed not by a distant enemy, but by someone close to him.
He did not disguise the pain.
He brought it before God.
That is one of the most overlooked aspects of biblical faith.
Surrender is not emotional dishonesty.
You can tell God that you are angry.
You can confess that you want revenge.
You can admit that you are struggling to forgive.
You can pray through tears and tell Him that you do not understand why the person who hurt you seems to be prospering.
God already knows what is inside your heart.
Prayer is not the performance of emotions you think a Christian should have.
It is bringing your actual heart into the presence of the God who already sees it.
And sometimes the first step toward freedom is simply telling the truth.
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I wanted them to suffer."
"Lord, I keep replaying what happened."
"Lord, I know You are just, but I am struggling to trust You."
"Lord, I don't know how to let this go."
That kind of honesty is not the opposite of faith.
It may be the beginning of a deeper surrender.
Because the God who calls you to release vengeance is not unfamiliar with injustice.
He entered a world filled with it.
And He experienced it personally.
Consider Jesus.
The sinless Son of God was betrayed by someone who shared His table.
Judas did not betray Him from a distance.
He approached Him with a kiss.
A gesture of affection became an instrument of treachery.
Then came false accusations.
Mockery.
Spitting.
Violence.
A crown of thorns.
A cross.
And through it all, Jesus remained righteous.
Peter later wrote:
"Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously."
—1 Peter 2:23, KJV
The Greek phrase at the end is particularly powerful:
παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως
Paredidou de tō krinonti dikaiōs.
"But He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly."
The verb paredidou conveys the act of handing over or entrusting. In this setting, it describes Jesus entrusting Himself and His cause to the righteous Judge.
Jesus did not retaliate.
He entrusted Himself to His Father.
But do not mistake His restraint for weakness.
The One who refused personal retaliation is the same Christ to whom the Father has entrusted judgment (John 5:22–27).
His refusal to strike back did not mean that evil had escaped divine justice.
It meant that His obedience was governed by the Father's will rather than the violence of His enemies.
And then, from the cross, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
—Luke 23:34, KJV

These words appear in the traditional text reflected by the King James Version, though some early Greek manuscripts omit this sentence. Its message is consistent with the mercy Jesus demonstrated and taught throughout His ministry.
Think about the extraordinary contrast.
Human cruelty was on full display.
And Christ responded with intercession.
But the cross was not merely an example of admirable self-control.
It was the place where the innocent Savior gave Himself for sinners.
The Bible tells us that Christ died for our sins (1 Corinthians 15:3).
He bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).
This is where the Gospel confronts our desire for vengeance with something far more unsettling.
We are not only people who have been wronged.
We are also sinners who need mercy.
That does not erase the distinction between victim and offender in any particular situation. It does not make every wrong equally severe or make an abused person responsible for their abuse.
But before the holiness of God, none of us can stand on the basis of our own sinlessness.
We have all sinned (Romans 3:23).
We have all needed grace.
And the Christian's hope is not that God has ignored sin.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has dealt with sin through His death and resurrection.
At the cross, mercy was not purchased by pretending evil was insignificant.
It came at an immeasurable cost.
And now the Savior who gave Himself for you calls you to release the vengeance that threatens to consume you.
Not because your wound doesn't matter.
But because your soul matters too.
Perhaps this is the hardest truth in the entire conversation.
Sometimes revenge feels like the last evidence that our pain mattered.
We think, "If I stop being angry, it's like saying what they did was okay."
"If I stop wanting consequences, it's like admitting I deserved it."
"If I forgive, they'll win."
But forgiveness is not a verdict that declares the offender innocent.
Forgiveness is a decision to relinquish personal vengeance while trusting God with ultimate justice.
It may begin before your emotions have caught up.
It may require repeated prayer.
It may coexist with grief, boundaries, and a legitimate pursuit of accountability.
It may be difficult to extend, especially when the harm was profound.
And it does not automatically restore trust.
Trust concerns a person's demonstrated reliability.
Reconciliation concerns the restoration of a relationship.
Forgiveness concerns the posture of your heart toward the wrong committed against you.
They are related, but they are not identical.
Romans 12:18 recognizes that peace does not depend entirely on one person:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Scripture acknowledges that peace is not always within your power to achieve.
You cannot force another person to repent.
You cannot manufacture genuine remorse.
You cannot rebuild trust on behalf of someone who continues to deceive you.
And you cannot create a safe relationship by pretending danger does not exist.
But by God's grace, you can begin surrendering the desire to retaliate.
That surrender is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like closing the social media page you keep checking.
Sometimes it means refusing to spread a damaging rumor, even when you know the other person has spread lies about you.
Sometimes it means seeking wise counsel rather than plotting humiliation.
Sometimes it means reporting wrongdoing through appropriate channels without making cruelty your objective.
Sometimes it means praying, through clenched teeth, "Lord, I want justice. Help me not to become unjust while I wait."
And sometimes it means grieving what will never be restored in this life.
Because there are losses that an apology cannot reverse.
There are betrayals that permanently change relationships.
There are consequences that remain even after forgiveness.
The Bible does not promise that every broken relationship will be repaired before heaven.
But it does promise that God will ultimately judge with righteousness.
And it calls His people to live in light of that promise.
Consider David again.
Before he became king, Saul repeatedly sought to kill him.
David had opportunities to retaliate.
In 1 Samuel 24, Saul entered a cave where David and his men were hiding.
David could have killed him.
His companions saw the opportunity as providential.
But David refused to seize the throne through vengeance.
He said:
"The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee."
—1 Samuel 24:12, KJV
David was not saying Saul had done nothing wrong.
He confronted Saul's actions.
He defended his innocence.
And he continued taking precautions against danger.
Yet he refused to take revenge into his own hands.
That is the distinction.
He trusted God's judgment without surrendering wisdom.
And perhaps that's what you need today.
Not a command to stop feeling pain.
Not another person telling you to "just move on."
Not pressure to return to the place where you were harmed.
But permission to stop carrying a responsibility that never belonged to you.
You were never appointed the final judge of another human soul.
You were never given the power to make the past unhappen.
You were never commanded to spend the rest of your life ensuring that someone else experiences enough suffering to balance yours.
God has not asked you to carry that burden.
And the longer you hold it, the heavier it becomes.
There is a profound difference between remembering a wrong and living under its rule.
One acknowledges history.
The other allows history to govern the present.
And through the transforming grace of Jesus Christ, that rule can begin to be broken.
Perhaps not all at once.
Perhaps not without counseling, pastoral care, prayer, or the help of trustworthy people.
Perhaps not without days when old anger returns.
But healing does not require pretending the wound was small.
It requires bringing the wound into the light of a Savior who is greater than it.
Listen to Paul's words just a few verses after "Vengeance is mine."
"Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
—Romans 12:21, KJV
What a remarkable command.
Not merely "Avoid revenge."
Not merely "Keep your anger under control."
But do not let evil overcome you.
The Greek verb translated "overcome" comes from nikaō, meaning to conquer or prevail over.
Paul presents a spiritual conflict.
Evil seeks to overcome you.
Not only through the original act of wrongdoing, but also through the temptation to respond in kind.
If someone lies about you and you begin lying about them, evil has multiplied.
If someone humiliates you and you make humiliation your mission, evil has found another instrument.
If someone becomes cruel and you surrender your character to cruelty, the original injustice has produced another tragedy.
But when you refuse retaliation and pursue what is righteous, something different happens.
The evil remains evil.
Yet it does not get to determine your obedience.
You may not be able to change what someone did to you, but by God's grace, what they did does not have to decide who you become.
This is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
This is the transforming work of Christ in a surrendered life.
And it brings us to a question that may be uncomfortable.
What if the person you want God to punish eventually repents?
What if the one who betrayed you turns to Jesus Christ?
What if the one who lied about you becomes genuinely broken over their sin?
What if the one who harmed you receives the mercy of God?
Would you rejoice that a sinner had been rescued?
Or would part of you feel cheated?
That question reaches deep into the human heart.
Because sometimes we don't merely want justice.
We want to control who receives mercy.
The prophet Jonah struggled with this.
God sent him to Nineveh, a city associated with wickedness and violence.
When the people repented and God showed mercy, Jonah was angry.
He knew God was gracious and merciful.
And that was precisely what troubled him.
Jonah wanted judgment.
God demonstrated His willingness to show mercy to the repentant.
The story exposes a tension we often carry.
We want God's mercy for ourselves.
But sometimes we want His strictest judgment for the people who hurt us.
Yet the Gospel does not belong to us to distribute according to our personal preferences.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
And if an offender genuinely repents and trusts in Jesus Christ, God's grace is sufficient to forgive that sinner.
That does not mean earthly consequences automatically disappear.
It does not mean victims must resume relationships.
It does not mean repentance can be reduced to words without fruit.
But it means the mercy of God is greater than our desire to decide who deserves it.
And we should be grateful.
Because if grace were only for people who had never deeply wounded anyone, what hope would there be for sinners?
Think of Saul of Tarsus.
He persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He dragged believers from their homes.
And yet the risen Jesus confronted him.
The persecutor became an apostle.
The man who once tried to destroy the church became a servant of the Gospel.
That is not a sentimental story about a man improving himself.
It is a testimony to the power of Jesus Christ.
From rebellion to surrender.
From spiritual blindness to the proclamation of the risen Lord.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical truth of what happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by eliminating every earthly consequence.
But by redeeming sinners, transforming hearts, and bringing hope where judgment seemed to be the only possible ending.
And now consider something even more personal.
What if the deepest freedom God wants to give you isn't the satisfaction of seeing your offender fall?
What if it is the ability to live faithfully even if you never witness their downfall?
What if your peace no longer depended on their apology?
What if their public reputation stopped determining your private stability?
What if you could hear their name without feeling compelled to rehearse the entire injury?
What if your prayers became less consumed with what God should do to them and more attentive to what He is doing in you?
Not because they were right.
But because Christ is Lord.
Not because the injustice was small.
But because God's justice is perfect.
Not because forgiveness is easy.
But because His grace is sufficient for the difficult road of obedience.
And please understand something.
You may not be there yet.
You may still be crying.
You may still need help.
You may still be angry.
You may still be taking necessary steps to protect yourself and others.
That does not mean your story is beyond redemption.
It means you are a human being walking through something painful.
And the Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).
He does not require you to manufacture a triumphant testimony before you have finished grieving.
He invites you to come to Him truthfully.
With the anger.
With the confusion.
With the questions.
With the memories.
With the trembling faith.
With the desire for justice.
Bring it all.
And ask Him to teach you the difference between pursuing what is right and clinging to what is vengeful.
There is a prayer you may need to pray today.
Not because it is easy.
Not because the person who hurt you deserves your silence.
Not because you have stopped caring about justice.
But because you are beginning to recognize that vengeance cannot heal the wound it promises to avenge.
"Father, You saw what happened.
You know the words that were spoken, the trust that was broken, and the damage that remains.
You know what others do not know.
You know the truth even where people have believed lies.
I confess that sometimes I have wanted revenge more than healing.
Sometimes I have imagined their humiliation.
Sometimes I have measured Your goodness by whether they appeared to suffer.
Forgive me for the ways bitterness has begun to shape my heart.
Teach me to seek justice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
Give me courage to speak the truth, wisdom to establish boundaries, and strength to take the right steps where protection and accountability are needed.
Where I am afraid, help me.
Where I am angry, meet me.
Where I am wounded, heal me according to Your wisdom.
And where I have begun to sit in the place that belongs only to You, help me surrender.
I entrust my cause to the One who judges righteously.
Not because I understand everything.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of my trust.
In His name, amen."
Maybe you couldn't pray every word of that sincerely.
That's okay.
Begin with the words you can honestly say.
"Lord, help me want to surrender."
Sometimes that is where the journey begins.
And if this message has uncovered something you've been carrying in silence, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You don't have to reveal names, private details, or painful experiences you're not ready to share.
You can also share a testimony of how Jesus helped you forgive without denying the truth of what happened.
Your honesty might encourage someone who has spent years believing that struggling to forgive means God has abandoned them.
Not as a replacement for Scripture, prayer, wise counsel, or necessary support, but as a reminder to return to Romans 12:19–21 when anger threatens to take over.
Read those verses for yourself.
Let God's Word examine your heart.
Not to publicly shame an offender.
Not to send a passive-aggressive message.

But because somewhere among your family, friends, and followers, there may be a person quietly drowning in resentment who desperately needs to know that surrendering vengeance is not the same as surrendering justice.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in the mission behind these messages.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing emotional stories.

Our desire is to point people to the living Christ, encourage serious engagement with Scripture, call sinners to repentance, strengthen weary believers, and remind the brokenhearted that the Gospel is still good news.

We want these resources and Gospel-centered messages to continue reaching people who might never walk into a church building, people who are searching for answers in the middle of the night, and people who are one honest prayer away from beginning a new chapter of faith.
For believers who choose to give this way, it can be part of their intentional Christian generosity and support for Gospel ministry.

Scripture encourages believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). The Bible also teaches the importance of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
But if you believe in what Gospel Warrior is doing, and God has given you the willingness and ability to support it, your partnership can help us keep serving others.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Christ is.
You are still welcome here.
Your salvation is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is the Savior, and salvation is by grace through faith, not by purchasing access to religious content (Ephesians 2:8–9).
What we are inviting you into is partnership, not spiritual obligation.
And perhaps that is fitting for an article about surrender.
Because everything we have belongs ultimately to God.
Our time.
Our influence.
Our resources.
Our gifts.
Even the painful stories we wish had never happened.
We can bring all of it before Him and ask, "Lord, how can this life glorify You?"
Sometimes the answer involves giving.
Sometimes it involves serving.
Sometimes it involves speaking the truth.
Sometimes it involves protecting the vulnerable.
And sometimes it involves the quiet, unseen obedience of refusing to repay evil with evil.
But before you leave, I want you to return to the question we began with.
What is God asking you to give up when you've been wronged?
Not your memory.
Not your dignity.
Not your right to seek lawful justice.
Not your ability to establish boundaries.
Not the truth.
He is calling you to surrender personal vengeance.
To stop treating retaliation as the only possible proof that your pain matters.
To stop allowing another person's sin to become the governing power of your life.
To trust that the righteous Judge sees what human eyes overlook.
And to follow the Savior who suffered injustice without becoming unjust.
Maybe the person who wounded you will repent.
Maybe they will apologize.
Maybe the truth will come out.
Maybe earthly justice will be done.
Or maybe you will never see the ending you hoped for.
But none of those uncertainties can overturn the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
The cross tells us that God does not dismiss evil as insignificant.
The empty tomb tells us that evil and death do not have the final word.
And the returning Christ assures us that history is moving toward the righteous judgment of God (Acts 17:31).
So you can stop trying to become the final author of someone else's consequences.
You can entrust judgment to God.
You can pursue what is right.
You can seek help.
You can grieve honestly.
You can learn to forgive.
You can begin again.
And by the grace of Jesus Christ, you can refuse to let the darkest thing someone did to you become the defining thing about you.
Because your story is not ultimately about the person who betrayed you.
It is about the Savior who will never betray you.
The One who was wounded for our transgressions.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who will judge the world in righteousness.
The One who is still transforming lives.
And if you're standing at the crossroads between bitterness and surrender, hear this one final time.
You do not have to hold the gavel to be heard by the Judge.
